title: Forms and User Input
description: Build a form with correctly labeled input controls, understand name vs. id, choose appropriate input types, and fix a label-association mistake.

objectives.statement: Explain what an HTML form is used for and what the name attribute does compared to id.
Build a form with labeled input controls, correctly associating each label to its control via matching for/id values, and include a submit control.
Identify and fix a basic form-structure or label-association mistake.

content.title: Forms and User Input
content.hook: A form with unlabeled inputs works fine for you, because you can see the placeholder text. For a screen reader user, it's a wall of unlabeled boxes.
content.context: Forms are how a page collects information — and label association is the single most common thing beginners get wrong.
goals: Build a form with correctly associated labels

content.title: Forms Collect Input — Labels Explain It
content.text: A <form> collects user input through controls like <input>, <select>, and <textarea>. Every control needs an associated <label> so anyone — sighted or using a screen reader — knows what it's for. That association isn't automatic: it happens by setting the label's for attribute to match the control's id exactly. The id and name attributes look similar but do different jobs: id uniquely identifies an element on the page (used for label association, styling, or scripting), while name identifies the field when the form is submitted — it's the key a server actually receives. They are not interchangeable, and a control commonly needs both. A submit control (<button type="submit"> or <input type="submit">) triggers the form's submission.

callout.text: Placing a label visually next to an input is not the same as associating it. Without a matching for/id pair, a screen reader has no reliable way to connect them.

content.keyTakeaway: id connects a label to its control; name is what the server sees when the form is submitted.

content.question: What is the key difference between an input's `id` and its `name`?

options.text: There is no difference — they're interchangeable.
`id` uniquely identifies the element on the page (e.g. for label association); `name` is the key sent to the server on submission.
`name` is only used for styling; `id` is only used for JavaScript.
`id` is required only on `<form>` itself, not on individual controls.

content.explanation: id is about identifying the element in the page (including for label association); name is about what key/value pair the server receives when the form submits.

feedback.correct: Right — id is for identifying the element, name is for the submitted data.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite — think about what a label needs to connect to versus what a server actually receives.

content.title: Fix the Unassociated Label
content.prompt: This form's label is placed right next to the input, but clicking the label text doesn't focus the input, and a screen reader won't announce the connection. Find and fix the mistake.
content.buggyCode:
<form>
  <label>Email Address</label>
  <input type="email" id="email-field" name="email">
  <button type="submit">Sign Up</button>
</form>
content.bugDescription: The label has no for attribute, so it isn't actually associated with the input despite sitting next to it visually.
fixRequirements: The label's for attribute must match the input's id exactly (email-field)
content.solutionCode:
<form>
  <label for="email-field">Email Address</label>
  <input type="email" id="email-field" name="email">
  <button type="submit">Sign Up</button>
</form>
hints: Look at the input's id value — the label needs a for attribute matching it exactly.

feedback.correct: Right — now the label and input are genuinely associated, not just visually adjacent.
feedback.incorrect: Check that the label's for value matches the input's id value exactly.

content.title: Build a Labeled Signup Form
content.prompt: Build a form with a labeled text input for 'Full Name', a labeled email input for 'Email', and a submit button labeled 'Sign Up'. Every label must be correctly associated with its input.
content.instructions: Use matching for/id pairs, appropriate input types, and a submit control.
content.solutionCode:
<form>
  <label for="full-name">Full Name</label>
  <input type="text" id="full-name" name="fullName">
  <label for="email">Email</label>
  <input type="email" id="email" name="email">
  <button type="submit">Sign Up</button>
</form>

testCases.description: Two labels present, each with a for attribute
Each label's for matches an existing input id
Two labels present, each with a for attribute
Each label's for matches an existing input id

feedback.correct: That's a properly labeled, accessible form.
feedback.incorrect: Check that every label has a for value matching a real input id, and that a submit control exists.

content.title: What You Should Take Away
takeaways: Every form control needs a label explicitly associated via matching for/id values.
id identifies an element on the page; name is the key the server receives on submission — they aren't interchangeable.
Visual proximity between a label and a control is not the same as real association.
